name: inception_v4

members.name: InceptionV4Config
members.signature: InceptionV4Config(num_classes: int = 1000, in_channels: int = 3, dropout: float = 0.2)
members.extended:
Inception-v4 is a single-size architecture: the paper (Figure 9)
defines exactly one network, so this configuration carries only the
input / output widths and the head dropout.  Every channel count and
repeat count inside the body is fixed by the paper.

parameters.name: num_classes
parameters.description: Width of the classifier head (ImageNet-1k by default).

parameters.name: dropout
parameters.description:
Drop probability applied to the pooled features before the
classifier.  Figure 9 specifies *keep* probability 0.8, i.e. a
drop probability of 0.2.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models.vision.inception_v4 import InceptionV4Config
>>> cfg = InceptionV4Config()
>>> cfg.model_type
'inception_v4'
>>> cfg.num_classes, cfg.in_channels, cfg.dropout
(1000, 3, 0.2)
notes:
This is the *TF-Slim* Inception-v4 — the network the released
checkpoint was trained as — which follows the paper's figures in
every channel width and repeat count.  One detail is dictated by the
released tensors rather than by the drawings: where a figure lists an
asymmetric factorised pair ($1\times7$ then $7\times1$,
or $1\times3$ then $3\times1$) in one order and TF-Slim
builds the other, the TF-Slim order is used, because the checkpoint's
weight shapes fix it.

Layout as built (`299×299` input):

  - Stem (Figure 3):  299×299×3  → 35×35×384
  - 4× Inception-A:   35×35×384
  - Reduction-A:      35×35×384  → 17×17×1024  (k, l, m, n = 192, 224, 256, 384)
  - 7× Inception-B:   17×17×1024
  - Reduction-B:      17×17×1024 →  8×8×1536
  - 3× Inception-C:    8×8×1536
  - AdaptiveAvgPool → Dropout(p=0.2) → Linear(1536, num_classes)

Every convolution is followed by `BatchNorm2d(eps=1e-3)` (the
TF-Slim default) and a ReLU.

parameters.description: Input images of shape `(B, in_channels, H, W)`.

members.extended:
Implements the non-residual network of Szegedy et al., "Inception-v4,
Inception-ResNet and the Impact of Residual Connections on Learning",
AAAI 2017 (Figure 9): the multi-branch stem of Figure 3, four
Inception-A modules, Reduction-A, seven Inception-B modules,
Reduction-B, and three Inception-C modules.  Designed for
$299\times299$ RGB inputs, which it maps to an
$8\times8\times1536$ feature map.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description:
Frozen architecture spec.  Use `inception_v4` for the
paper configuration.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.inception_v4 import inception_v4
>>> backbone = inception_v4().eval()
>>> x = lucid.randn(1, 3, 299, 299)
>>> backbone.forward_features(x).shape
(1, 1536, 8, 8)
>>> [f.num_channels for f in backbone.feature_info]
[64, 160, 384, 1024, 1536]
notes:
Every module is a filter concatenation of parallel branches,



$$
y = \operatorname{concat}\big(\mathcal{B}_1(x), \dots,
    \mathcal{B}_k(x)\big),
$$

with no residual shortcut anywhere — that is what separates
Inception-v4 from its sibling Inception-ResNet.  The trunk holds
41.1 M parameters; the paper reports 20.0% top-1 / 5.0% top-5
single-crop error on the ImageNet validation set for the full
classifier.

attributes.name: config
attributes.description: Stored copy of the config that built this model.

attributes.name: features
attributes.description:
The 22-module trunk: `features.0`–`features.5` are the stem,
`6`–`9` Inception-A, `10` Reduction-A, `11`–`17`
Inception-B, `18` Reduction-B and `19`–`21` Inception-C.

attributes.name: feature_info
attributes.description:
One entry per stage boundary — channels 64 / 160 / 384 / 1024 /
1536 at reductions 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 / 32.

members.name: InceptionV4ForImageClassification

methods.name: reset_classifier
methods.summary: Replace the classification head with a freshly initialised one.
methods.extended:
The head keeps the checkpoint's `last_linear` attribute name, so
this cannot come from `ClassificationHeadMixin` (which looks for
`self.classifier`).

methods.name: forward
methods.signature: forward(x: Tensor, labels: Tensor | None = None)

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Input images of shape `(B, in_channels, H, W)`.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description:
Integer class targets of shape `(B,)`.  When given, the
cross-entropy loss is returned alongside the logits.

members.summary: Inception-v4 image classifier (trunk + GAP + dropout + linear).
members.extended:
Adds the paper's head to the `InceptionV4` trunk: global
average pooling over the $8\times8$ grid, dropout with keep
probability 0.8 (`config.dropout = 0.2`), and a single
`lucid.nn.Linear` layer producing `config.num_classes`
logits.  The trunk is held directly as `features` and the head as
`last_linear` so the state dict matches the released checkpoint's
keys one-for-one.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description:
Architecture spec.  Use `inception_v4_cls` for the paper
configuration.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.inception_v4 import inception_v4_cls
>>> model = inception_v4_cls().eval()
>>> out = model(lucid.randn(2, 3, 299, 299))
>>> out.logits.shape
(2, 1000)
notes:
The loss, computed only when `labels` is given, is the mean
categorical cross-entropy



$$
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N}
    \log \operatorname{softmax}(\text{logits}_n)_{\,y_n}.
$$

42.7 M parameters in total.  The paper reports 20.0% top-1 / 5.0%
top-5 single-crop error on the ImageNet validation set (Table 2).

attributes.description: Stored copy of the config that built this model.

members.extended:
Inception-v4 trains with a single softmax head — the paper drops the
auxiliary classifiers of GoogLeNet / Inception v3 — so this dataclass
carries only the logits and an optional loss.

parameters.name: loss
parameters.description:
Mean cross-entropy against `labels` when they were passed to
`InceptionV4ForImageClassification.forward`; `None`
otherwise.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.inception_v4 import inception_v4_cls
>>> model = inception_v4_cls().eval()
>>> out = model(lucid.randn(1, 3, 299, 299))
>>> out.logits.shape
(1, 1000)
>>> out.loss is None
True

members.name: inception_v4
members.extended:
Builds an `InceptionV4` with the topology of Szegedy et al.
2017, Figure 9: multi-branch stem → 4× Inception-A → Reduction-A →
7× Inception-B → Reduction-B → 3× Inception-C, ending in an
$8\times8\times1536$ feature map for a $299\times299$
input.  41.1 M parameters (the published classifier's 42.7 M less
its 1536 → 1000 head).

parameters.name: pretrained
parameters.description:
No pretrained weights are published for the headless backbone;
`True` raises `NotImplementedError` rather than returning
a randomly initialised model.  The ImageNet-1k checkpoint belongs
to `inception_v4_cls`, which the error message names.

returns.description:
Backbone with the Inception-v4 configuration applied (or with
`overrides` merged on top of it).

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.inception_v4 import inception_v4
>>> model = inception_v4().eval()
>>> out = model(lucid.randn(1, 3, 299, 299))
>>> out.last_hidden_state.shape
(1, 1536, 8, 8)
notes:
See Szegedy et al., "Inception-v4, Inception-ResNet and the Impact of
Residual Connections on Learning", AAAI 2017.  The paper defines a
single network, so there are no size variants (H11).

members.name: inception_v4_cls
members.signature: inception_v4_cls(pretrained: bool | str = False, weights: InceptionV4Weights | None = None, overrides: object = {})
members.summary: Inception-v4 image classifier (trunk + GAP + dropout + linear).
members.extended:
Builds an `InceptionV4ForImageClassification` with the paper's
topology and head — global average pool, dropout with keep
probability 0.8, and a `lucid.nn.Linear` layer producing
`config.num_classes` logits.  42.7 M parameters, matching the
released TF-Slim ImageNet checkpoint.

parameters.name: pretrained
parameters.description:
Pretrained-weight selector.  `False` → random init; `True`
→ the `DEFAULT` tag (`InceptionV4Weights.TF_IN1K`); a tag
string (e.g. `"TF_IN1K"`) → that specific checkpoint.  Mutually
exclusive with `weights` (which wins if both are given).

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description:
Explicit weights enum member, e.g. `InceptionV4Weights.TF_IN1K`.
Takes precedence over `pretrained`.

parameters.name: **overrides
parameters.description:
Keyword overrides forwarded into `InceptionV4Config`.
Common picks: `num_classes=N` to retarget the head,
`dropout=p` to change the head regularisation.  Overriding
`num_classes` away from the checkpoint's 1000 makes pretrained
loading fail the strict key/shape check — load with the matching
head, then call `reset_classifier`.

returns.description:
Classifier with the Inception-v4 configuration applied (or with
`overrides` merged on top of it), optionally initialised from
pretrained weights.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.inception_v4 import inception_v4_cls
>>> model = inception_v4_cls(num_classes=10).eval()
>>> out = model(lucid.randn(2, 3, 299, 299))
>>> out.logits.shape
(2, 10)
Load ImageNet-pretrained weights:
>>> model = inception_v4_cls(pretrained=True)
>>> from lucid.models.weights import InceptionV4Weights
>>> model = inception_v4_cls(weights=InceptionV4Weights.TF_IN1K)
notes:
See Szegedy et al., "Inception-v4, Inception-ResNet and the Impact of
Residual Connections on Learning", AAAI 2017.  Single-crop ImageNet
validation error reported in Table 2: 20.0% top-1 / 5.0% top-5.  The
head is named `last_linear` so the TF-Slim checkpoint's keys load
unchanged.

Pretrained weights are converted from timm's `inception_v4.tf_in1k`
— the TensorFlow-Slim ImageNet-1k checkpoint — and hosted on the
Hugging Face Hub under `lucid-dl/inception-v4`.  timm reports
80.144% top-1 / 94.982% top-5 for it at 299x299 with the preset that
`InceptionV4Weights.TF_IN1K.transforms` reproduces (299 crop,
341 resize, bicubic, `(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)` mean/std — the TF-Slim
$[-1, 1]$ scaling, not the ImageNet statistics).

members.name: InceptionV4Weights
members.extended: Szegedy et al. AAAI 2017 (42.7 M params, top-1 80.14%).
examples:
>>> from lucid.models.weights import InceptionV4Weights
>>> InceptionV4Weights.DEFAULT is InceptionV4Weights.TF_IN1K
True
>>> tf = InceptionV4Weights.TF_IN1K.transforms()
>>> tf.crop_size, tf.resize_size, tf.interpolation
(299, 341, 'bicubic')
>>> tuple(tf.mean), tuple(tf.std)
((0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
notes:
Reference: Szegedy, Ioffe, Vanhoucke, Alemi, *"Inception-v4,
Inception-ResNet and the Impact of Residual Connections on
Learning"*, AAAI 2017 ([arXiv:1602.07261](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.07261)).

attributes.name: TF_IN1K
attributes.description:
TensorFlow-Slim ImageNet-1k checkpoint (top-1 80.144% / top-5
94.982% at 299, per timm's `results-imagenet.csv` for this
exact tag), sourced from `timm/inception_v4.tf_in1k`.  The
paper's Table 2 reports 80.0% / 95.0% single-crop for its own
evaluation.

citation: Szegedy, Christian, et al. "Inception-v4, Inception-ResNet and the Impact of Residual Connections on Learning." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, vol. 31, no. 1, 2017, pp. 4278–4284.
theory:
Inception-v4 is the purely *non-residual* member of the 2016
Inception generation.  Where Inception v3 had grown piecemeal —
each stage partitioned differently so the model could be trained
across many machines under memory limits — Inception-v4 re-draws the
whole network as a *uniform* design: one fixed stem, three kinds of
Inception module repeated in blocks, and two dedicated reduction
modules between them.  Every module is a set of parallel branches
whose outputs are concatenated along the channel axis,



$$
y = \operatorname{concat}\big(
    \mathcal{B}_1(x),\ \mathcal{B}_2(x),\ \dots,\ \mathcal{B}_k(x)
\big),
$$

where each branch $\mathcal{B}_i$ is a short chain of
convolutions (or a pooling followed by a $1\times1$
projection), each followed by batch normalisation and a ReLU.

The layout is Stem → 4× Inception-A ($35\times35\times384$) →
Reduction-A → 7× Inception-B ($17\times17\times1024$) →
Reduction-B → 3× Inception-C ($8\times8\times1536$) → global
average pool → dropout (keep 0.8) → linear classifier.  The stem
itself is multi-branch: three filter-concatenation junctions take a
$299\times299$ image to a $35\times35\times384$ grid, and
every spatial reduction in it runs a stride-2 convolution and a
stride-2 max pool side by side instead of choosing one.  Large
kernels are factorised throughout — an $n\times n$ convolution
becomes a $1\times n$ followed by an $n\times1$, which
covers the same receptive field for $2n$ rather than
$n^2$ weights per input–output channel pair.

The paper's point in building Inception-v4 alongside
Inception-ResNet was a controlled comparison: with a comparable
compute budget, residual connections speed training up markedly but
are *not* what makes a very deep Inception network accurate —
Inception-v4 reaches roughly the accuracy of Inception-ResNet-v2
(single-crop top-5 error 5.0% on the ImageNet validation set,
against 4.9%) with no shortcuts at all.
